## Overview

A cellular automaton is a grid of cells, each in one of a few states, updated
in discrete time steps. At every step each cell looks at its own state and the
states of its neighbours and applies the same **local rule** to decide its next
state [@CeccheriniSilberstein2010]. Simple rules can produce strikingly complex
behaviour.

In `CellularAutomataCore.jl` a simulation has four ingredients:

| ingredient | example |
|---|---|
| a **rule** | `Wolfram(30)`, `Life()`, or any function |
| an **initial state** | an array, e.g. `single_seed(101)` |
| a **time span** | a number of steps, e.g. `50` |
| a **space** (optional) | a ring or torus the size of the state, by default |

They are bundled into a `CAProblem` and run with `solve`.

```{julia}
#| output: false
ENV["GKSwstype"] = "100"  # headless plotting
using CellularAutomataCore
using Plots
using Random
```

## A first automaton: rule 30

Elementary cellular automata live on a line of cells with two states, `0` and
`1`. Each cell's next state depends on itself and its left and right
neighbours. There are $2^3 = 8$ possible neighbourhoods, so a rule is a table of
8 bits; Wolfram's numbering reads that table as a binary number. Rule 30 is the
table `00011110`.

```{julia}
u0 = single_seed(101)   # 101 cells, all 0 except the centre
prob = CAProblem(Wolfram(30), u0, 50)
sol = solve(prob)
```

`sol.u` holds the saved states and `sol.t` their times. By default every step
is saved, so there are 51 states, from `t = 0` to `t = 50`.

```{julia}
length(sol.u), sol.t[1], sol.t[end]
```

Plotting a one-dimensional solution draws a space-time diagram: one row per
time step, time running downwards.

```{julia}
plot(sol; c=:binary, colorbar=false, size=(700, 380), title="Rule 30")
```

The same data as a single array, with time as the **last** axis:

```{julia}
size(trajectory(sol))
```

## Other elementary rules

Rule 90 makes each cell the exclusive-or of its two neighbours. From a single
seed it draws Pascal's triangle modulo 2, the Sierpiński gasket:

```{julia}
plot(solve(CAProblem(Wolfram(90), single_seed(129), 63));
     c=:binary, colorbar=false, size=(700, 380), title="Rule 90")
```

Wolfram sorted elementary rules into four classes by their behaviour from
random initial states: uniform, periodic, chaotic and complex. Here is one
rule from each, on a ring of 150 cells started from the same random state:

```{julia}
u = Int8.(rand(Xoshiro(1), 0:1, 150))
panels = map([250, 108, 30, 110]) do code
    plot(solve(CAProblem(Wolfram(code), u, 100));
         c=:binary, colorbar=false, title="Rule $code", xlabel="", ylabel="")
end
plot(panels...; layout=(2, 2), size=(800, 600))
```

## Saving less, stepping by hand

Long runs need not keep every state. `saveat` saves every `k` steps (or at the
listed times); the first and last states are always kept.

```{julia}
sol = solve(CAProblem(Wolfram(110), u, 1000); saveat=250)
sol.t
```

For full control, `init` returns an integrator that advances with `step!`:

```{julia}
integ = init(CAProblem(Wolfram(30), single_seed(31), 100); saveat=1000)
step!(integ, 10)
integ.t, sum(integ.u)
```

## Two dimensions: the Game of Life

Conway's Game of Life is a two-state rule on a square grid. A dead cell with
exactly three live neighbours (out of its eight) is born; a live cell with two
or three live neighbours survives; every other cell dies or stays dead. It is
written `B3/S23`, for "born with 3, survives with 2 or 3".

A glider is a five-cell pattern that moves one cell diagonally every four
steps. Patterns are often shared in run-length-encoded (RLE) form:

```{julia}
glider, _ = parse_rle(raw"""
x = 3, y = 3, rule = B3/S23
bo$2bo$3o!
""")
glider
```

`place!` copies the pattern into an empty 20 × 20 board. The default space is
a torus, so the glider re-enters on the far side when it leaves the board.

```{julia}
u0 = place!(zeros(Int8, 20, 20), glider, (2, 2))
sol = solve(CAProblem(Life(), u0, 40); saveat=8)
plot([plot(sol; snapshot=i, c=:binary, colorbar=false) for i in 1:6]...;
     layout=(2, 3), size=(800, 540))
```

After 40 steps the glider has moved 10 cells down and 10 to the right:

```{julia}
final_state(sol) == circshift(u0, (10, 10))
```

From a random initial state Life settles into a mixture of still lifes,
oscillators and gliders:

```{julia}
soup = Int8.(rand(Xoshiro(42), 0:1, 120, 120))
sol = solve(CAProblem(Life(), soup, 300); saveat=10)
alive = [count(==(1), u) for u in sol.u]
plot(plot(sol; c=:binary, colorbar=false),
     plot(sol.t, alive; xlabel="t", ylabel="live cells", legend=false);
     layout=(1, 2), size=(800, 360))
```
